etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English sobben, perhaps from Middle Low German sabben (“to drool, slobber, salivate”). Cognate with West Frisian sabje, sobje (“to suck”), Dutch zabben, sabbelen (“to suck”), zabberen (“to drool”), German Low German sabbeln, severn (“to drool”), German sabbern (“to drool, slobber”), Norwegian sabbe (“to spill, drop, make a mess”). Compare also Old English sēofian (“to lament”), German saufen (“to drink, swig”).

definitions.definition: A cry with a short, sudden expulsion of breath.

quote.citation: 1874, George Carter Stent, The Jade Chaplet in Twenty-four Beads, page 9:
quote.text: “My husband, alas! whom I now (sob, sob) mourn,A short time since (sob) to this grave (sob) was borne;And (sob) he lies buried in this (sob, sob) grave.”

quote.citation: 1697, Virgil, “Pastoral 5”, in John Dryden, transl., The Works of Virgil: Containing His Pastorals, Georgics, and Æneis. […], London:  […]  Jacob Tonson, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: She sigh'd, she sobb'd, and, furious with despair, / She rent her garments, and she tore her hair.

quote.citation: 1707, J[ohn] Mortimer, The Whole Art of Husbandry; or, The Way of Managing and Improving of Land. […], London:  […]  J[ohn] H[umphreys] for H[enry] Mortlock […], and J[onathan] Robinson […], →OCLC:
quote.text: the Tree, being sobbed and wet, ſwells the Wood
